name: Vertical growth / downward growth

lead: Vertical growth, or downward growth, is looksmaxxing shorthand for a craniofacial pattern in which the upper and lower jaws develop with more height than forward projection. The result described is a longer lower face, a steeper jaw angle and a recessed look in profile. People use the term to analyse their own side photos and to work out what kind of change would improve their profile.

The idea overlaps with terms used in orthodontics, such as hyperdivergent or "long face" patterns and clockwise rotation of the jaws. Orthodontic literature links excessive vertical growth with mouth breathing and airway problems in children, and forum members connect it with habits such as tongue posture. Counter-clockwise rotation through jaw surgery is the option community members most often name for adults.

paras: In practice people photograph their profile, compare jaw angle and facial thirds, and discuss it on forums. Proposed responses include nasal breathing and tongue posture during growth years, orthodontic or orthopedic appliances, and surgical counter-clockwise rotation of the jaws, sometimes combined with a chin procedure. Surgical decisions are made with an orthodontist and maxillofacial surgeon.

The term is informal, so self-diagnosis from photos can differ from a clinician measurement. Jaw surgery carries the usual risks of major surgery, including swelling, numbness, relapse and a long recovery. Some forum members argue that taller jaws are attractive and that "forward growth" advice is misread, so views within the community differ.

angle.text: The concept gives people a way to describe why their profile looks long or recessed and to compare options such as breathing and posture habits, orthodontics or counter-clockwise jaw rotation surgery. Adults typically consider surgery, since growth-guidance habits are discussed mainly for the teenage years.

lead: Vertical growth, also called downward growth, is a term used in looksmaxxing communities for a facial growth pattern in which the maxilla and mandible develop more in height than in forward projection. Users describe it as producing a long lower third, a steep mandibular plane and a recessed-looking profile, and contrast it with "forward growth", where the jaws sit further forward relative to the skull. [1][2]

People use the concept as a diagnostic lens on their own side photos and as a way to decide what to work on: posture and breathing habits during the growing years, orthodontic or orthopedic appliances, or, for adults, surgical counter-clockwise (CCW) rotation of the jaws. Threads on looksmax.org ask whether nasal breathing and tongue posture between ages 14 and 20 can influence it and whether surgery is needed for adults. [1][2]

Orthodontics has its own vocabulary for a related pattern: hyperdivergent or "long face" growth, in which the maxillomandibular complex rotates downward relative to the cranial base. A longitudinal study of 371 people followed from age 6 to 20 described this growth trajectory in cephalometric terms. [3] A 2025 narrative review of pediatric sleep-disordered breathing lists excessive vertical growth, a constricted maxilla and a retruded, posteriorly rotated mandible among the craniofacial phenotypes associated with airway narrowing. [4]

The topic is bound up with orthotropics and mewing, the tongue-posture approach developed by British orthodontist John Mew and popularised by his son Mike Mew, who describes jaw growth in terms of whether the face grows down or forward. [5][6] Professional bodies do not endorse orthotropics, and the community itself disagrees about whether tall jaws are a flaw or an asset. [7][6]

paras: In community usage, downward growth means the maxilla, mandible or both have grown mainly downward, producing a taller lower face, a steeper jaw angle and less visible chin and cheek projection in profile. Members describe the opposite as forward growth.[1]

The wording is informal, and a thread on gonial angle shows users asking at what angle downward growth "begins", which indicates there is no agreed numeric cut-off. [8] Users commonly assess it from a side photo by looking at the slope of the lower jaw, the length of the lower third and how far the chin and cheeks sit forward, and some posters say ethnic background affects how a profile reads. [2]

The clinical counterpart is described as hyperdivergent growth, long face syndrome or skeletal open bite. Wikipedia summarises it as excessive vertical facial growth, usually with a steep lower occlusal and mandibular plane angle, often linked with vertical maxillary excess and a small lower jaw. It also notes that some experts dispute whether it should be called a syndrome at all. [9]

In the 2021 study by Knigge and colleagues in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics, researchers analysed five lateral cephalograms per person between ages 6 and 20 for 371 participants, grouped by adult mandibular plane angle into hyperdivergent (40), normodivergent (216) and hypodivergent (115) groups. In the hyperdivergent group the maxillomandibular complex rotated downward relative to the anterior cranial base, the lower anterior face grew proportionally more, and the jaws became relatively shorter and more posteriorly positioned with age. The authors noted that restricted maxillary growth in this pattern may raise the risk of Class II malocclusion. [3]
Clinicians distinguish this from forum shorthand: orthodontic diagnosis uses cephalometric radiographs and measurements rather than photographs, and treatment planning is individual. [3][9]

Forum posters frequently attribute downward growth to childhood mouth breathing and a low tongue position. One user who reported mouth breathing for about 13 years asked whether starting nasal breathing at 14 could still change it. A reply said posture could help some orthodontic issues slightly but would not fully reverse counter-clockwise rotation problems without orthodontics. [2]
Another thread laments that downward growth "could've been fixed" with better habits during development, and replies discuss CCW surgery as the priority for adults. [10]

The orthodontic literature links vertical growth patterns with pediatric sleep-disordered breathing; adenoid and tonsil enlargement are the most common causes, and residual breathing problems may be accompanied by craniofacial changes. [4] Wikipedia's long face syndrome article says both genetic and environmental factors are proposed, that researchers disagree about how environment interacts with genetics, and that mouth breathing in children is a recognised concern, though human findings are less consistent than animal studies. [9]

John Mew (1928 to 2025) founded orthotropics, which holds that malocclusion and facial form are shaped largely by posture, especially tongue and mouth posture, rather than genetics. He proposed that resting the tongue against the palate exerts an outward force that widens the upper jaw and keeps it from growing downward and backward. [5] Mewing, named for John and his son Michael Mew, is the popular version of this idea, and Google Trends interest rose from January 2019 as it spread through social media, including looksmaxxing communities. [6]

Mainstream orthodontic organisations do not support orthotropics. Wikipedia reports that the American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw, and that a 2019 review in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery found some plausible conclusions in Mew's theory but inadequate evidence of efficacy and concluded it is not a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery. [5][6] John Mew was reprimanded by the UK General Dental Council in 2010 over advertising and had his licence revoked in 2017; his son Mike was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and was struck from the UK dental register in 2024 after a misconduct hearing. [5][6]

Counter-clockwise rotation, usually by bimaxillary (double-jaw) surgery, is the option named most often for adults; users post before-and-after images of people who say it reduced the look of downward growth. [1]

Wikipedia's orthognathic surgery article states that a total maxilla osteotomy is used to treat long face syndrome, including vertical maxillary excess. It lists bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness (usually temporary) among possible complications, and describes initial healing over 2 to 6 weeks followed by 2 to 4 months of bone remodeling. [11]

For younger people, orthodontists use functional appliances in skeletal class II cases. A 2025 prospective cohort study measured hyoid bone position before and after functional orthodontic treatment, reflecting how muscle adaptation relates to jaw advancement. [12] For children with long face patterns, the stated goal of treatment is to control descent of the lower jaw and prevent posterior teeth from erupting too far, while severe adult cases may need orthodontics combined with orthognathic surgery. [9]

Not all users treat vertical growth as a problem. A post titled "Downward growth is good" argues that forward growth advice refers to the occlusal plane rather than literal jaw projection and that a tall, wide maxilla and lower third are features of attractive men. [7] Another thread argues that much perceived forward growth is really a lack of vertical growth. [13]
A further point of debate is timing: posters generally say posture habits matter in the growing years, while adults discuss surgery as the route that changes jaw position. [2][10]

No studies have tested the looksmaxxing concept of "downward growth" as such. Related orthodontic research covers vertical facial growth trajectories [3], vertical facial patterns and airway problems in children [4] and functional appliance outcomes in class II patients. [12] No controlled trial has shown that tongue posture or mewing changes vertical growth, and the professional bodies cited above describe the evidence as lacking. [5][6]

lore.intro: Downward growth is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, with threads asking whether it is fixable and how, and others arguing it is misunderstood. [1][2][7]
